title: Zephaniah 3:1–13
context: Zephaniah 3:1–13 turns back to Jerusalem, the rebellious and oppressing city that would not listen, accept correction, trust the LORD, or draw near to God. Her princes are roaring lions, her judges evening wolves, her prophets arrogant, and her priests have profaned the sanctuary. Yet the LORD within her is righteous and brings his justice to light every morning. The LORD says he cut off nations so that Jerusalem would fear him and accept correction, but they only grew more corrupt. He tells the faithful to wait for him until the day he gathers the nations to pour out his anger. Then he will purify the lips of the peoples so that all may call on his name and serve him together, and worshipers will come from beyond the rivers of Cush. He will remove the proud from Jerusalem and leave a humble and poor people who take refuge in his name; the remnant of Israel will do no wrong, speak no lies, and live without fear. Shared ground: both traditions read the remnant and the turning of the nations as God’s gracious work through judgment.

verses.text: Woe to her who is rebellious and polluted, the oppressing city!
verses.arminianNotes: Zephaniah pronounces woe on the rebellious, polluted, oppressing city. Arminian readers see the prophet turning from the nations to Jerusalem itself, showing that God’s people are not exempt from judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the shift as a warning to God’s own people. Both traditions note that the city is not named until verse 14, and they hold this as shared ground.

verses.text: She didn’t obey the voice. She didn’t receive correction. She didn’t trust in the LORD. She didn’t draw near to her God.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says the city did not obey, accept correction, trust the LORD, or draw near to God. Arminians see four failures that show a settled refusal to respond to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as describing the heart of rebellion. Both traditions hold this as shared ground: trust and nearness to God are the heart of faithfulness.

verses.text: Her princes within her are roaring lions. Her judges are evening wolves. They leave nothing until the next day.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says the city’s princes are roaring lions and its judges are evening wolves that leave nothing until morning. Arminian readers see leaders who prey on the people instead of protecting them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see corruption in leadership as a sign of a city under judgment. Both traditions compare Ezekiel 22:27 by reference, and they read the images as describing greed and oppression.

verses.text: Her prophets are arrogant and treacherous people. Her priests have profaned the sanctuary. They have done violence to the law.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says the city’s prophets are arrogant and treacherous, and its priests have profaned the sanctuary and done violence to the law. Arminians see spiritual leaders failing in their calling, leading the people astray.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the corruption of prophets and priests as especially serious. Both traditions compare Ezekiel 22:26 by reference, and they hold this as shared ground.

verses.text: The LORD, within her, is righteous. He will do no wrong. Every morning he brings his justice to light. He doesn’t fail, but the unjust know no shame.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says the LORD within the city is righteous, does no wrong, and brings his justice to light every morning, but the unjust know no shame. Arminian readers see God’s faithful presence contrasted with human corruption.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s justice as constant and unfailing. Both traditions hold this as shared ground: God’s righteousness stands even when his people fail.

verses.text: I have cut off nations. Their battlements are desolate. I have made their streets waste, so that no one passes by. Their cities are destroyed, so that there is no man, so that there is no inhabitant.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he has cut off nations and made their cities desolate. Arminians see God pointing to his judgment on the nations as a warning to Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty over the nations. Both traditions read the verse as showing that Jerusalem had clear examples of what happens to those who reject God.

verses.text: I said, “Just fear me. Receive correction,” so that her dwelling won’t be cut off, according to all that I have appointed concerning her. But they rose early and corrupted all their doings.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he told them to fear him and accept correction so their home would not be cut off, but they rose early to corrupt their deeds. Arminian readers see God’s sincere desire for repentance, which the people rejected.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that God’s call was sincere and see the people’s eager corruption as showing the depth of sin. Both traditions hold this as shared ground, and they read the verse as showing God’s patience before judgment.

verses.text: “Therefore wait for me”, says the LORD, “until the day that I rise up to the prey, for my determination is to gather the nations, that I may assemble the kingdoms to pour on them my indignation, even all my fierce anger, for all the earth will be devoured with the fire of my jealousy.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells them to wait for him until he rises to gather the nations and pour out his anger, for the earth will be consumed by the fire of his jealousy. Arminians see a call to the faithful to wait for God’s justice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s determination to judge the nations. Both traditions note that wait for me may be addressed to the humble remnant, and they read the verse as leading into the promise of verse 9.

verses.text: For then I will purify the lips of the peoples, that they may all call on the LORD’s name, to serve him shoulder to shoulder.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will purify the lips of the peoples so they may call on his name and serve him together. Arminian readers see God’s grace enabling the nations to worship him, an act they believe still invites response, as in the Deuteronomy 5:29 box.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s purifying work as effective, making true worship possible, as discussed in the Deuteronomy 10:16 box. Both traditions hold the gathering of the nations as shared ground and compare the reversal of Babel (Genesis 11).

verses.text: From beyond the rivers of Cush, my worshipers, even the daughter of my dispersed people, will bring my offering.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that from beyond the rivers of Cush his worshipers, the daughter of his dispersed people, will bring his offering. Arminians see the scattered people and distant nations coming to God in worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s gathering of his people from far places. Both traditions note that it is unclear whether these worshipers are scattered Israelites or Gentiles, and they hold the question open.

verses.text: In that day you will not be disappointed for all your doings in which you have transgressed against me; for then I will take away out from among you your proudly exulting ones, and you will no more be arrogant in my holy mountain.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that on that day they will not be put to shame for their sins, for he will remove the proud from among them. Arminian readers see God’s forgiveness and his removal of pride as the way to restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s cleansing work as making his people new. Both traditions hold this as shared ground: God removes both the guilt and the arrogance that marked his people.

verses.text: But I will leave among you an afflicted and poor people, and they will take refuge in the LORD’s name.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will leave among them an afflicted and poor people who take refuge in his name. Arminians see the remnant as those who humbly trust God, continuing the call to seek him in 2:3.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the remnant as preserved by God’s grace. Both traditions hold the humble remnant as shared ground, and they read taking refuge in the LORD’s name as the mark of true faith.

verses.text: The remnant of Israel will not do iniquity nor speak lies, neither will a deceitful tongue be found in their mouth, for they will feed and lie down, and no one will make them afraid.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the remnant of Israel will do no wrong, speak no lies, and live without fear. Arminian readers see a transformed people whose lives reflect God’s character, living in security.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s work of renewal producing holiness. Both traditions note the shepherd imagery of feeding and lying down, and they hold this as shared ground.
